title: The Town Clock Debate
passage: In the center of Aki's town stood a clock tower built almost eighty years ago. The clock had once been an important public service, but nearly everyone now carried a phone. When the town announced that the mechanism needed an expensive repair, some residents questioned whether the clock was still worth maintaining. The debate seemed simple at first: either spend public money on an old object or use the money for something more useful. Aki's civics class decided to study the issue. They began by asking residents what the tower meant to them. Older people often described it as a landmark connected with memories of festivals and school trips. Shop owners said visitors used it as an easy meeting point. Younger residents were less attached to the clock itself but liked the open square around it. A few people argued strongly against repair, pointing out that the town also needed money for road maintenance and child-care services. The students then examined the repair estimate. They learned that there were several options rather than one fixed cost. Replacing the entire mechanism would be expensive but reliable. Repairing only the damaged parts would cost less now but might require another repair later. A third option was to stop the clock while preserving the tower as a monument. Each choice changed both cost and function. The class invited a local historian and an engineer to speak. The historian warned that once working parts were removed, restoring the original function in the future could become difficult. The engineer explained that old equipment sometimes required custom parts, which increased cost, but also noted that regular maintenance could extend its life. Neither expert told the students what the town should do. Instead, they described consequences that were easy to miss. Aki's group proposed a public survey, but their teacher asked how the survey would be designed. If the question simply asked, Should we repair the clock, people might answer differently depending on whether they knew the price or the alternatives. The students created a longer form showing three options with estimated costs and likely future maintenance. The results did not produce an overwhelming winner. The lowest-cost repair received the most support, but many comments asked the town to seek private donations rather than paying entirely from taxes. Eventually, the town chose that approach. It funded basic safety work, while a local association raised money for the clock mechanism. The solution did not remove all criticism. Some residents believed public heritage should be fully supported by taxes, while others thought no public money should be used at all. Aki learned that disagreement does not always disappear after more information is provided. People can understand the same facts and still value goals differently. Yet better information can improve the quality of disagreement by making trade-offs visible. The clock now works again, but for Aki the more important lesson was how public choices are shaped not only by facts, but also by the way questions are framed and by what communities decide is worth preserving.
translation: 秋の町の中心には、約八十年前に建てられた時計塔がありました。かつては重要な公共設備でしたが、今ではほとんどの人がスマートフォンを持っています。高額な修理が必要だと分かると、『古い物に税金を使うより他の用途に回すべきだ』という意見が出ました。秋の公民の授業ではこの問題を調べることになりました。住民に聞くと、高齢者は祭りや学校行事の記憶と結びついた象徴として語り、商店主は待ち合わせ場所として役立つと言いました。若者は時計そのものへの思い入れは弱くても、周囲の広場を好んでいました。一方、道路整備や子育て支援を優先すべきだという反対意見もありました。さらに修理費を調べると、全交換、部分修理、時計を止めて塔だけ保存するという複数の案があり、費用と機能がそれぞれ異なりました。歴史家は、動く機能を失うと将来の復元が難しくなる可能性を指摘し、技術者は古い機械は特注部品で高くなる一方、定期整備で寿命を延ばせると説明しました。生徒たちは住民アンケートを提案しましたが、先生は質問の作り方が答えを左右すると指摘します。単に『修理すべきか』と聞くのではなく、三つの案、費用、将来の維持費を示して調査しました。結果は圧倒的ではなく、低コストの部分修理が最も多かったものの、税金だけでなく寄付を募る案も多く寄せられました。最終的に町は安全面の基本工事を公費で行い、機械部分は地域団体が寄付を集めました。それでも、文化財は税金で守るべきだという人も、税金を一切使うべきでないという人も残りました。秋は、情報が増えれば必ず意見が一致するわけではないと学びます。同じ事実を理解しても、何を大切にするかは異なるからです。ただし、選択の代償を見える形にすれば、議論の質は高められます。時計は再び動き始めましたが、秋にとって本当の学びは、公共の選択が事実だけでなく、問いの立て方や地域が何を残す価値があると考えるかによって形づくられることでした。

title: A School Without Bells
passage: When Seaside Junior High renovated its buildings, the principal proposed an unusual experiment: for one month, the school would stop using bells between most classes. Students would still have a visible schedule, and teachers would keep clocks in every room, but the familiar sound would disappear except for emergency signals. Supporters argued that students should learn to manage time rather than depend on a bell. Critics predicted chaos. Some teachers worried that classes would run late, while parents questioned whether younger students were ready for so much responsibility. During the first week, the critics seemed partly correct. Several classes ended late, and some students arrived after the next lesson had begun. Teachers also discovered that their classroom clocks were not perfectly synchronized. The school could have ended the experiment immediately, but the principal asked staff to identify which failures came from the idea itself and which came from poor preparation. The school synchronized clocks, placed large time displays in hallways, and asked teachers to give a two-minute warning before class ended. Students were encouraged to check the schedule during breaks instead of waiting for a sound. By the second week, late arrivals decreased. An unexpected change also appeared: corridors became calmer because hundreds of students no longer moved at exactly the same second. Some teachers allowed students to finish a final sentence before leaving, while others ended slightly early when an activity was complete. However, the experiment created new concerns. A student with attention difficulties said the bell had provided an important external reminder. Another student worried constantly about the time and checked the clock too often. In response, the school offered optional vibration timers and visual reminders. The debate then shifted. The question was no longer simply whether bells were good or bad, but how much structure different students needed. At the end of the month, the school surveyed students, teachers, and families. Most students preferred fewer bells, but many wanted a sound before lunch and at the end of the school day. Teachers were divided. Some valued the flexibility, while others felt that time management had become an extra task competing with instruction. The school adopted a mixed system: no bells between ordinary morning classes, but signals at several major transition points. Seaside's experiment did not prove that every school should remove bells. Its conditions mattered. The building was small enough that students could move quickly, clocks were visible, and staff spent time adjusting the system. A larger school might have different results. The principal emphasized this point in the final report. Educational experiments are sometimes discussed as if one successful example provides a universal answer, but local context changes what is practical. The real value of the experiment was not that it discovered the perfect bell schedule. It showed the school which functions the bells had been serving: coordination, reminders, reassurance, and control of movement. Once those functions were visible, the community could decide which ones should remain and which students could manage in other ways.
translation: シーサイド中学校が校舎改修をした際、校長は一か月間、授業間のチャイムをほとんど鳴らさない実験を提案しました。時間割と時計は残し、緊急時の信号だけは別にします。賛成派は、生徒がチャイムに頼らず時間管理を学ぶべきだと考え、反対派は授業の遅れや混乱を心配しました。最初の週は実際に授業が延びたり、次の授業に遅れる生徒が出たりし、教室ごとの時計がずれていることも判明しました。しかし校長は、失敗が考え方そのものによるのか、準備不足によるのかを分けて考えるよう求めました。時計を同期し、廊下に大きな表示を置き、教師が終了二分前に知らせるようにすると、遅刻は減りました。また全員が同時に動かないため廊下が落ち着くという予想外の利点もありました。一方、注意を保つのが難しい生徒にとってチャイムは重要な外部の合図であり、逆に時間を気にしすぎて何度も時計を見る生徒もいました。そこで振動タイマーや視覚的なリマインダーを選べるようにしました。議論は『チャイムが良いか悪いか』ではなく、『人によってどの程度の外部構造が必要か』へ変わりました。最終調査では生徒の多くがチャイム減少を好みましたが、昼食前や一日の終わりには合図が欲しいという声が多く、教師の意見は分かれました。学校は通常の午前授業間は鳴らさず、大きな切り替えの時だけ鳴らす混合方式を採用しました。この実験は全学校でチャイムをなくすべきだと証明したわけではありません。校舎の大きさ、時計の見やすさ、調整に使える時間など条件が違えば結果も変わります。重要だったのは完璧なチャイム制度を見つけたことではなく、チャイムが『時間の調整、注意喚起、安心感、人の移動をそろえること』という複数の機能を持っていたと明らかになったことでした。その機能が見えたことで、何を残し、何を別の方法に置き換えるか考えられるようになったのです。

title: The Data Behind the Cafeteria Menu
passage: The cafeteria at Mari's school wanted to reduce the amount of food thrown away after lunch. Staff began weighing leftovers from each dish and recording the results. After a month, one pattern looked obvious: vegetable dishes produced more waste than rice or bread. A quick response would have been to serve fewer vegetables. However, the nutrition teacher warned that the data showed what students left, not why they left it. The student council joined the investigation. They compared waste with menu type, serving size, weather, and the order in which dishes were placed on the serving line. They also conducted a short anonymous survey. The results complicated the original story. One vegetable dish was unpopular because it became watery when kept warm for too long. Another was generally liked, but the serving spoon was large, so students often took more than they wanted. On days when a new dish appeared, waste was high because students could not judge how much to take. The council tested several changes. For familiar vegetables, they used smaller serving spoons and allowed students to return for more. For new dishes, they offered a small tasting portion first. Kitchen staff also changed the preparation time of the watery dish so it spent less time warming. Waste fell during the test, but another issue appeared. Allowing second servings created a short line, and students with later lunch periods worried that popular dishes might run out. Staff therefore prepared a small reserve and monitored demand. Mari noticed that each improvement created a new condition to consider. The project was not a simple search for the single cause of waste. It was a system in which portion size, taste, timing, expectations, and food supply interacted. The school also had to avoid an unintended goal: reducing waste by making students take too little food. Nutrition mattered more than producing an impressive waste number. For that reason, the final report included two measures instead of one: leftover weight and the percentage of students who reported being satisfied with the meal. The council also tracked whether students returned for second servings. After a term, vegetable waste had decreased, while satisfaction remained roughly stable. The school considered this encouraging but did not call the project finished. Menus changed with the seasons, and new students would arrive the following year. Mari learned that numbers are powerful when they help people notice patterns, but a number does not explain itself. If the school had reacted only to the first chart, it might have reduced vegetables and claimed success while making lunches less healthy. Better decisions came from combining measurement with observation, questions, and small experiments. She also learned that a metric can influence behavior. Once people are told to minimize one number, they may find ways to improve it that do not serve the real purpose. The cafeteria's true goal was not the lightest trash bin. It was to provide nutritious meals that students would actually eat while wasting as little food as reasonably possible.
translation: 真理の学校の食堂では、昼食後に捨てられる食品を減らすため、料理ごとの残り物を量って記録し始めました。一か月後、野菜料理の廃棄が米やパンより多いことが明らかになりました。単純に考えれば野菜を減らせばよいように見えますが、栄養担当の先生は『データが示すのは何を残したかで、なぜ残したかではない』と指摘しました。生徒会は、献立、盛り付け量、天気、配膳順などと廃棄量を比べ、匿名アンケートも行いました。すると、ある野菜料理は保温時間が長く水っぽくなること、別の料理は味は好評でも大きなスプーンで取りすぎること、新しい料理では適量が分からず残しやすいことが分かりました。そこで小さなスプーン、追加のおかわり、新料理の少量試食、調理時間の変更などを試しました。廃棄は減りましたが、今度はおかわり列ができ、後半の時間帯で料理が不足する不安が出たため、少量の予備を用意しました。真理は、一つ改善すると新しい条件が現れ、この問題が単一原因ではなく、量、味、時間、期待、供給が関係する仕組みだと気づきました。また『廃棄を減らす』だけを目標にすると、生徒に少なすぎる量を取らせれば数字だけは良くなる危険もあります。そこで最終報告では廃棄重量だけでなく、食事への満足度とおかわり状況も測りました。一学期後、野菜の廃棄は減り、満足度はほぼ維持されました。ただし季節や新入生によって状況は変わるため、終了とは考えませんでした。真理は、数字はパターンを見つける力を持つ一方、数字自身が理由を説明するわけではないと学びます。最初のグラフだけで判断していれば、野菜を減らして数字を改善しながら昼食を不健康にしていたかもしれません。測定、観察、質問、小さな実験を組み合わせることでより良い判断ができます。そして本当の目的は『ごみ箱を最も軽くすること』ではなく、栄養のある食事を生徒が実際に食べ、無理のない範囲で無駄を減らすことでした。

title: The Translation Club's Difficult Choice
passage: A volunteer translation club at Yuto's school helped prepare English information for international visitors. At first, members believed accurate translation meant replacing each Japanese sentence with the closest English sentence possible. Their first major task was a guide to a local summer festival. The Japanese guide contained traditional terms, polite expressions, and references that local readers understood without explanation. When the club translated the text directly, the English sounded grammatical, but several exchange students found it confusing. One sentence described a portable shrine using a cultural term with no familiar English equivalent. Another politely warned visitors about entering a restricted area, but the direct translation sounded so indirect that readers did not understand it as a warning. The club debated what to do. One group wanted to preserve the original expressions as closely as possible because changing them might erase cultural meaning. Another wanted to rewrite freely so visitors could understand the practical message. Their adviser asked them to separate two kinds of accuracy: accuracy to the form of the original and accuracy to the effect the message needed to have. Neither could always be maximized at the same time. The club tested several solutions. For important cultural terms, they kept the Japanese word in Roman letters and added a short explanation the first time it appeared. For safety instructions, they used clearer and more direct English than the Japanese wording. For a historical paragraph, they kept more of the original structure because readers had time to read slowly. The students also asked exchange students to review the guide without seeing the Japanese. Their comments revealed problems the translators had missed. A sentence that seemed simple to club members used the word local in a way that made visitors wonder whether only residents were allowed to participate. Another section used the word traditional so often that it lost meaning. Yuto learned that translation was not a puzzle with one correct answer for each sentence. It required decisions about audience, purpose, context, and what information could safely be assumed. The final guide included a short note explaining that some cultural terms were left in Japanese intentionally. During the festival, volunteers observed how visitors used the guide. Most questions concerned transportation and event times rather than cultural vocabulary, so the next edition moved practical information to the front. The club's work gradually expanded from translation to communication design. They considered headings, order, maps, and the amount of explanation readers needed. Yuto came to see that faithful communication sometimes requires moving away from the surface form of the original. A warning that nobody recognizes as a warning is not successful simply because every word was translated closely. At the same time, making everything familiar to foreign readers could remove the very cultural difference the guide was meant to introduce. The club's goal became balance: preserve what matters, explain what may be unfamiliar, and make essential actions unmistakably clear.
translation: 悠斗の学校の翻訳ボランティア部は、海外からの来訪者向け英語案内を作っていました。最初は、日本語の各文をできるだけ近い英語に置き換えることが正確な翻訳だと考えていました。しかし夏祭りの案内を直訳すると、文法は正しくても交換留学生には分かりにくい部分が多く残りました。神輿のように英語にぴったり対応する語がない文化語や、日本語では丁寧でも英語では警告だと気づきにくい立入禁止表現などです。部内では、元の表現を守るべきだという意見と、実用性を優先して自由に書き換えるべきだという意見に分かれました。顧問は、『原文の形への正確さ』と『相手に必要な効果を与える正確さ』を分けて考えるよう促しました。両方を常に最大にすることはできません。文化的に重要な語はローマ字で残し、初出時に短い説明を加える。安全案内は日本語より直接的にする。歴史説明は時間をかけて読めるため原文構造を多めに残す、といった使い分けをしました。また日本語原文を見ていない留学生に読んでもらうと、『local』の使い方から地元住民しか参加できないと誤解しそうな箇所や、『traditional』の使いすぎなど、部員が気づかなかった問題も見つかりました。悠斗は、翻訳は各文に一つの正解があるパズルではなく、読者、目的、状況、前提知識を考える作業だと学びました。祭り当日に観察すると、文化語より交通や時間の質問が多かったため、次版では実用情報を前に移しました。活動は次第に翻訳だけでなく、見出し、情報順序、地図、説明量を考えるコミュニケーション設計へ広がりました。言葉を忠実に置き換えても警告と伝わらなければ十分ではありません。一方、すべてを外国人に馴染みのある形に直せば、紹介したい文化の違いが消えてしまいます。大切なものは残し、未知のものは説明し、必要な行動は明確にする。そのバランスが部の目標になりました。

title: The Shortcut Through the Field
passage: For years, students walking to East Hill School used an unofficial shortcut across an empty field. The path saved about seven minutes compared with the public road. Nobody had built it; repeated footsteps had simply created a narrow line through the grass. When the land was sold for development, a fence blocked the route. Students complained immediately. Some climbed around the fence until teachers warned them that the land was private and construction would soon begin. The obvious answer seemed to be that students should accept the longer legal route. However, the sudden change revealed a larger problem. The public road had a narrow sidewalk, heavy morning traffic, and a crossing where cars turned quickly. Parents who had never worried about the field path became concerned. The school asked the city to examine the walking route. Traffic engineers counted vehicles and observed students during arrival time. They confirmed that the road met legal safety standards, but they also noted that large groups of students created crowding not reflected in average pedestrian counts. The developer, meanwhile, argued that the construction site could not remain open as a passage because of safety and insurance risks. Some residents blamed the developer for removing a community route, while others pointed out that the path had crossed private land without formal permission for years. A city planner explained the idea of a desire path: when many people repeatedly choose the same informal route, their behavior can reveal a need that official planning has not fully addressed. This did not automatically give the public a right to use private land, but it provided useful evidence about where people wanted to travel. The city explored several alternatives. Building a completely new public path would require purchasing land and take years. Adding a crossing guard every day would have ongoing costs. Changing the timing of one traffic signal and widening a short section of sidewalk could be done sooner. The developer also agreed to leave a narrow strip along one edge of the property that might later connect to a public path, although it would remain closed during construction. The immediate solution was modest: the signal timing changed, temporary staff supervised the busiest crossing for several weeks, and the school staggered arrival recommendations by a few minutes. The seven-minute shortcut did not return. Still, the city added the future path connection to its neighborhood plan. For Ryo, a student involved in the discussions, the experience changed how he thought about rules and systems. The field path had been unofficial, yet it carried information. Hundreds of people had independently chosen it because the official network did not match their preferred movement. At the same time, popularity alone could not erase property rights or construction dangers. Ryo learned that useful planning requires taking informal behavior seriously without pretending it settles every legal or safety question. Sometimes a worn line in the grass is not merely people breaking a rule; it is also data about a need that the formal map has missed.
translation: イーストヒル校の生徒たちは長年、空き地を横切る非公式の近道を使っていました。公道より約七分短く、誰かが作ったのではなく、人が歩き続けたことで草の中に自然に道ができたものです。土地が売却され、工事用の柵で閉じられると生徒は不満を言いました。私有地なので長い公道を使えばよいように見えましたが、変更によって別の問題が表面化しました。公道は歩道が狭く、朝の交通量が多く、車が速く曲がる横断場所もありました。市の調査では法律上の安全基準は満たしていましたが、登校時間に大人数の生徒が集中する状況は平均的な歩行者数では十分表せていないことが分かりました。開発業者は安全や保険の問題から工事現場を通路にできないと説明し、住民の中には業者を責める人もいれば、そもそも長年正式な許可なく私有地を通っていたと指摘する人もいました。都市計画担当者は、多くの人が繰り返し非公式の経路を選ぶことでできる『欲求の道』という考えを説明しました。それは私有地を通る権利を自動的に生むわけではありませんが、公式の道路網が満たしていない移動需要を示す情報になります。市は新しい公共道、毎日の見守り、信号時間変更、歩道拡幅などを比較しました。新道は土地購入に時間がかかり、見守りには継続費用が必要です。そこで短期的には信号時間を変え、一時的な見守り員を置き、登校時刻を少し分散する対策を行いました。業者も将来の公共道につながる細い土地を残すことに同意しました。七分の近道は戻りませんでしたが、将来の接続路は地域計画に加えられました。議論に参加した涼は、非公式の道でも重要な情報を持つと学びました。多くの人がそこを選んだのは、公式の道路が実際の移動希望に十分合っていなかったからです。ただし人気があるだけで所有権や工事安全の問題を無視することはできません。草に残った一本の道は、単なる規則違反ではなく、地図が見落としていた需要を示すデータでもあるのです。

title: The Air Conditioner Problem
passage: During an unusually hot June, students at Hoshi Junior High complained that several classrooms felt uncomfortable even though the air conditioners were running. The school office responded by lowering the temperature setting. Electricity use rose sharply, yet complaints continued. A science teacher suggested that the school investigate before lowering the setting further. Students in an environmental club borrowed simple temperature and humidity sensors and placed them in different parts of the building. They expected to find broken machines. Instead, the measurements revealed large differences within the same classroom. Desks near sunny windows were several degrees warmer in the afternoon, while areas directly under air outlets felt cold. In one room, the sensor near the teacher's desk showed a comfortable temperature even when students by the windows felt hot. The club also measured carbon dioxide levels as a rough sign of ventilation and found that rooms became stuffy when doors and windows remained closed for long periods. Opening windows improved ventilation but allowed hot outdoor air inside, making cooling harder. The problem was not a single setting. The school tested several changes. Reflective shades were installed on the hottest windows. Fans were used to mix air so cooled air did not remain concentrated in one area. Short ventilation periods were scheduled between lessons instead of leaving windows partly open all the time. Teachers were asked to keep doors closed while cooling unless ventilation was taking place. The school then returned the air conditioner settings closer to their original level. Comfort improved in many rooms, and electricity use fell compared with the first hot week. However, the club avoided claiming that the new system was universally best. Rooms on different floors received different amounts of sun, weather changed daily, and personal comfort varied. One student felt cold at a temperature another considered perfect. The school therefore added a simple reporting form so repeated problems in particular rooms could be identified rather than treating every complaint with the same adjustment. Mina, a club member, was especially interested in what had gone wrong at the beginning. Lowering the temperature setting seemed like a direct response to a heat complaint, but it assumed the air conditioner itself was the main cause. Because no one had measured conditions across the room, the first solution used more energy without addressing uneven sunlight, air movement, or ventilation. Mina began to see a general pattern. When a problem is described by one visible symptom, people often change the most obvious control. Sometimes that works. Other times, the symptom is produced by several interacting factors. Measurement helps separate those possibilities. Yet measurement also has limits: a sensor can report temperature, but it cannot fully measure whether a student feels comfortable, tired, or distracted. The school's final approach combined physical data with human reports. Mina concluded that efficient problem-solving does not mean trusting numbers instead of people or people instead of numbers. It means using each source to answer the kinds of questions it can answer well.
translation: 非常に暑い六月、星中学校では冷房が動いているのに教室が不快だという苦情が続きました。学校は設定温度を下げましたが、電力使用量だけが急増し、不満はなくなりませんでした。科学の先生の提案で環境部が温度・湿度センサーを教室各所に置くと、故障ではなく同じ教室内で大きな差があることが分かりました。午後の日当たりの強い窓際は数度高く、吹き出し口の真下は寒く感じられました。先生の机付近が適温でも窓側の生徒は暑い場合もありました。また換気の目安として二酸化炭素濃度を測ると、窓や扉を長く閉めると空気がこもる一方、窓を開け続ければ暑い外気が入り冷房効率が落ちます。つまり単一の設定温度の問題ではありませんでした。学校は、日当たりの強い窓に反射シェードを付け、扇風機で空気を混ぜ、授業間に短時間換気を行い、冷房中は換気時以外ドアを閉める方法を試しました。その後設定温度を元に近づけても快適さは改善し、最初の猛暑週より電力消費も減りました。ただし階や日当たり、天候、個人差があるため一つの方法が全教室に最適とは言いませんでした。同じ温度でも寒い人と快適な人がいるからです。そこで教室ごとの繰り返し問題を把握できる報告フォームも作りました。部員の美奈は、最初の失敗に注目しました。暑いという症状に対し設定温度を下げるのは直接的に見えますが、原因が冷房能力だと決めつけていました。教室内を測定しなかったため、日射、空気の偏り、換気を改善せずエネルギーだけ増やしたのです。目立つ症状に対して最も分かりやすい操作を変えるだけで解決することもありますが、複数要因が絡む場合もあります。測定はその違いを見分ける助けになります。ただしセンサーは温度を測れても、生徒の快適さや疲労を完全には測れません。学校は物理データと人の感覚の両方を使いました。効率的な問題解決とは、数字か人のどちらか一方を信じることではなく、それぞれが得意な問いに使うことだと美奈は結論づけました。
